transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-05-20 14:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-20260520-ps-4932 (note: link shared in chat)

Summary (auto): quick check-in on model routing options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), context length tradeoffs (8k vs 32k), multilingual fidelity (EN/ES/JA), and tool-calling (DB/function) reliability. Agreed to run hosted eval and share benchmarks; DE/SE to follow up on Dedicated pricing and private deployment docs.

Topics: model selection, context length, multilingual, tool-calling, VPC/on-prem constraints, SOC2/KMS, latency vs cost tradeoffs, caching and batching strategies.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Samira Kaur: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samira from Redwood. Quick roll call, and then we can jump in.
[00:00:09] Markus Li: Markus here, PelagoSoft. Hi.
[00:00:11] Aisha Rahman: Aisha — ML lead.
[00:00:13] Jon Cabrera: Jon, platform.
[00:00:15] Lena Ortiz: Lena, product.
[00:00:18] Diego Ramos: Diego from Redwood SE.
[00:00:20] Nina Patel: Nina on solutions engineering.
[00:00:22] Samira Kaur: Great. Agenda is short: we wanted to follow up on the model routing choices you mentioned last week, dig into context lengths — you brought up 8k vs 32k — and figure out the best path for tool-calling and multilingual. Is that still right?
[00:00:34] Markus Li: Yep, that's the gist. We've been prototyping with an in-house stack but it's getting expensive and flaky at scale. Two immediate constraints: a lot of our queries need long context — user chat history plus documents — sometimes hitting 20k tokens; second is we need strong Spanish and Japanese support.
[00:00:48] Aisha Rahman: And reliability on function-calls — we call external microservices and vector DB ops a lot, so deterministic function/tool calling is important.
[00:00:56] Jon Cabrera: Also our security team prefers VPC or on-prem for PII-heavy flows.
[00:01:01] Samira Kaur: Got it. Quick outline: we'll compare model families for long context and multilingual, then talk deployment modes — hosted, Dedicated reserved pools, and Private (VPC/on-prem) — and finally tooling (function calling, vector DB integrations, caching). Sound good?
[00:01:14] Lena Ortiz: Yep.

[00:01:20] Diego Ramos: I'll start with the model bit. For open models that we've validated, the practical picks for 8k/32k style workloads are Mistral-family variants and Llama 3-type variants, plus a few specialized long-context forks. In our hosted catalog we show performance profiles — like throughput, average latency, and token-cost estimates — but there can be significant differences once you add tool-calling or streaming.
[00:01:45] Aisha Rahman: When you say "Mistral", is that the mainline Mistral or the long-context forks? Because we tried a community long-context patch and it had kv cache bugs.
[00:01:54] Diego Ramos: Good call. We generally recommend the long-context verified builds — we tag them in the catalog as longctx-8k or longctx-32k. There are a few community builds we avoid; they often mis-handle the KV cache leading to growth in memory. Our runtime has some KV cache protections but it depends on the model compiling correctly.
[00:02:10] Nina Patel: Also, for multilingual, Llama 3 derivatives tend to be strong on Spanish, but Japanese sometimes requires a model with dedicated pretraining or fine-tuning. We often suggest a hybrid approach: use one primary model for most lat-lingual stuff and route Japanese-heavy prompts to a model tuned for CJK.
[00:02:27] Markus Li: Router rules — are they per-request? We want deterministic routing based on detected language and estimated prompt length. Ideally not adding a big latency tax.
[00:02:36] Diego Ramos: Yes, our smart routing runs a tiny classifier at the edge (sub-millisecond) — it can route by language, token estimate, cost bucket, or customer tier. The routing itself is lightweight; the biggest latency hit is when you route to a 32k model vs an 8k model which may be on different node pools.
[00:02:50] Jon Cabrera: Are those node pools in Dedicated only or hosted too?
[00:02:54] Nina Patel: We run both in hosted, but in Dedicated you can pin pools to GPUs that are better at long-context (more memory) to keep latency stable. For Private (VPC/on-prem) you control the hardware and we provide the runtime.

[00:03:08] Lena Ortiz: Talk about cost — our CFO is sensitive here. 32k models seem expensive. Is that just tokens or also memory/warm up charges?
[00:03:16] Diego Ramos: All of the above. Per-token costs rise with sequence length but the big jump is GPU memory and GPU time for KV cache and attention. Also, batching behavior changes. With 32k contexts you often get lower batch sizes which reduces throughput efficiency — so unit cost increases. We can show quantization and batching profiles that reduce cost while keeping quality.
[00:03:34] Aisha Rahman: What's your experience with prefix caching? We have repeated doc snippets across sessions; could caching reduce our 20k active window?
[00:03:42] Diego Ramos: Yes, prefix and KV caching is one of the biggest wins. If a chunk of the context is static (policy text, previous transcripts), Redwood can cache and reuse KV across requests, reducing token computation. There are tradeoffs with freshness and cache invalidation, but for static policy docs it's great.
[00:03:56] Markus Li: Nice. For tool-calling — we need guaranteed exactly-once semantics for some ops (billing calls). How deterministic is your function-calling?
[00:04:05] Samira Kaur: Short answer: function calls are deterministically triggered based on model output, but network retries can cause duplicates. We provide idempotency hooks and a small library pattern to make calls idempotent. The other thing is you can run function-calling in the private network for sensitive calls, or route only the final call payload through a private connector.
[00:04:22] Jon Cabrera: So the flow would be model -> Redwood runtime determines function call -> we provide connector -> call executes in our VPC?
[00:04:29] Nina Patel: Exactly. With Private deployments we can install a connector inside your VPC so the runtime does the function invocation without leaving the network. For hosted we provide secure tunnels but that depends on your compliance needs.

[00:04:40] Aisha Rahman: Any caveats with streaming and function-calls together? We stream token-level results to the UI and also sometimes need a late-bound function call after stream completes.
[00:04:49] Diego Ramos: Streaming plus tool-calling is supported but the sequence matters. If you want an early function call mid-generation, we convert that event into a structured output and trigger the connector. Late-bound calls after final token generation are more straightforward. There can be minor ordering discrepancies on retries — we document patterns to reconcile them.

[00:05:05] Markus Li: On reliability — what's your SLA on hosted vs Dedicated?
[00:05:09] Samira Kaur: Hosted has high availability but no single-tenant SLA. Dedicated includes SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; Private gets the enterprise control so you set the operational SLAs with our support package. For PelagoSoft-sized deployments we usually recommend Dedicated for predictable latency, unless your compliance team insists on Private.
[00:05:27] Lena Ortiz: Our security folks asked about KMS and HSM — can Redwood integrate with our KMS for key material?
[00:05:33] Nina Patel: Yes, we integrate with standard KMS providers and can work with HSM-backed key stores in Private deployments. Hosted supports envelope encryption and customer-managed keys for certain plans; we'll share the integration guide.

[00:05:45] Jon Cabrera: Any gotchas when moving from hosted eval to Private? We've got an air-gapped cluster for PII.
[00:05:51] Diego Ramos: The main differences are: network topology and connectors (no outbound, so we bundle a connector), and you might need to provide the exact GPU types. Also, the control plane can be customer-managed in Private, which requires a short install window. We have an on-prem checklist for that.

[00:06:06] Aisha Rahman: For multilingual fidelity — do you recommend one model or multi-model routing? Latency-sensitive paths prefer one model to avoid routing overhead.
[00:06:15] Nina Patel: There's no one-size-fits-all. For high-volume core flows, pick a strong multilingual base model. For niche languages like Japanese where quality drops, route to a tuned model. Our routing penalties are small but non-zero — usually <10ms for the classifier — so it's often worth it.

[00:06:30] Markus Li: Can we run an experiment where 80% of traffic hits a single multilingual model and 20% routed to specialized models for QA comparison?
[00:06:36] Samira Kaur: Absolutely. We can do traffic split rollouts and A/B your prompt set. That's a typical canary.

[00:06:44] Jon Cabrera: On monitoring, what telemetry do we get for token-level costs and tool-call failures?
[00:06:49] Diego Ramos: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost breakdowns per-route, per-model, and per-token type. We also surface failed tool-calls, latencies, and retry counts. You can connect to Datadog or send logs to your SIEM.

[00:06:59] Lena Ortiz: Any sample numbers you can share now for p50/p95 latency on 8k vs 32k?
[00:07:05] Diego Ramos: Rough ballpark: for a mid-sized model (longctx-8k) on hosted, p50 ~ 120ms for 1-2 token steps (short generation), p95 around 380ms for typical responses. For 32k variants p50 jumps to ~280ms and p95 to 1.2s depending on seq length and batching. These are estimates; we'll run your prompts to get concrete numbers.

[00:07:26] Aisha Rahman: That p95 variance matters. We'll need numbers on token cost and also per-call cost when function-calls are included.

[00:07:33] Samira Kaur: We'll provide a benchmark spreadsheet mapping your sample prompts to latency/cost on candidate models. Diego will run the hosted eval with your samples.

[00:07:40] Markus Li: About the hosted eval — what's the scope? Are we giving you credentials and sample prompts? And who provisions?
[00:07:47] Diego Ramos: Ideally you give a representative prompt set (Aisha will do that), some sample documents for context, and indicate which calls need tool-calling / DB hits. We'll run a 7-day run on hosted, capture latency/cost/quality, and then share the sheet. We'll also test prefix cache effectiveness with the static docs you provide.

[00:08:02] Aisha Rahman: We'll prepare a 50-query seed set and also top-200 anonymized queries.

[00:08:06] Nina Patel: Perfect. For the Dedicated pricing, Samira will send ranges but we typically present a few commitment tiers (monthly/annual) with reserved GPU pools tuned for long-context.

[00:08:16] Samira Kaur: Right. I'll send a deck and pricing ranges. Also attaching Security + On-prem checklist.

[00:08:22] Jon Cabrera: One more technical: you mentioned quantization to save cost — any quality hits with quantized long-context models?
[00:08:29] Diego Ramos: There's a tradeoff. Q4/INT8 quantization usually preserves generation quality for many tasks but can degrade some multilingual or numeric precision tasks. We recommend running your eval prompts in quantized and unquantized modes to measure delta. For high-sensitivity flows, we keep an unquantized model for a small percent of traffic.

[00:08:48] Markus Li: Good to know. Regarding retries and idempotency for billing calls — if a function-call fails mid-flight, how do you surface that in the transcript/console?
[00:08:56] Nina Patel: We track function-call status and retries in the request trace. There's an event stream for calls that failed and whether they were retried. We can hook webhooks into your system to surface those events immediately.

[00:09:08] Lena Ortiz: Any impacts to privacy/regulatory with caching? We sometimes store partial PII in context.
[00:09:14] Samira Kaur: You control retention. For hosted we default to short retention and opt-in longer retention for analytics; Dedicated/Private gives you full control. If you need zero retention we can enable that. Also note that caching static policy docs is fine; caching PII requires encryption and policy rules.

[00:09:28] Aisha Rahman: Ok, let's talk sequencing: we want to run hosted eval -> review benchmarks -> Dedicated pricing review -> possible Private install for PII-heavy subset. Does that flow make sense?
[00:09:37] Samira Kaur: Yes, that's the standard path. Many customers pilot on hosted then move to Dedicated or Private for production.

[00:09:42] Markus Li: Budget-wise we're aiming for a POC spend cap — we'll need approximate hosted cost per 100k tokens for 8k vs 32k.
[00:09:50] Diego Ramos: We'll include that in the benchmark. We can also provide a cost model spreadsheet so you can plug in expected traffic.

[00:09:57] Jon Cabrera: One logistical: our security wants the SOC 2 docs and details on where logs are stored.
[00:10:02] Samira Kaur: I'll attach SOC 2 and the data residency page. For logs we can send to your SIEM or redact at ingestion per route.

[00:10:11] Aisha Rahman: Cool. Anything else?
[00:10:13] Nina Patel: Two quick notes: 1) If you plan to push 20k+ contexts frequently, tell us your expected qps so we can size the Dedicated pool. 2) If you have multilingual fine-tuning data we can help with a small fine-tune or instruction tuning job in the eval phase.
[00:10:28] Markus Li: We aim for 25 qps at peak.
[00:10:31] Aisha Rahman: We'll share a small 2k-example fine-tune set.

[00:10:35] Samira Kaur: Great. Recap / Next steps: (1) Aisha share sample prompts + top-200 queries (due 5/24) (2) Diego run 7-day hosted eval and baseline tests (due 5/27) (3) Samira send Dedicated pricing and SOC2/on-prem guide (due 5/22) (4) Redwood share benchmark spreadsheet after run.
[00:10:54] Markus Li: Sounds good.
[00:10:56] Jon Cabrera: One follow up — can we get a short doc on cache invalidation patterns?
[00:11:01] Diego Ramos: Yes, I'll attach a one-pager on caching strategies.

[00:11:04] Lena Ortiz: Thanks, everyone.
[00:11:06] Samira Kaur: Thanks all. We'll follow up in email with links and timeline.
[00:11:10] (call ends, note: remainder of meeting was Q/A and quick screen share of Redwood Console — recording includes short demo clips)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-recognitions around product names ("Mistral" sometimes transcribed as "Miss-tral"), "KV cache" appears as "K V cache" at times, and some interrupted speech truncated lines.
